summary: Discusses how SRv6 can be applied to the user plane of mobile networks. Its network programming and statelessness can give flexibility, end-to-end network slicing, and SLA control. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Phone data traffic gets handled like a list of stops, which makes it simpler for the network to carry.

subtitle: Using Segment Routing over IPv6 to simplify the data plane of mobile networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile networks currently use GTP-U tunnels to separate user traffic by session, but tunneling adds overhead and complexity. Each session requires tunnel state, and traffic engineering is limited because the user plane and transport layer are rigidly separated.
tldr.mechanism: SRv6 applies Segment Routing to the IPv6 data plane, replacing GTP-U with a source-routing approach where the path and services are encoded in an ordered list of segments in the IPv6 Routing Header. Each segment can represent a UPF anchor, a service node, or a traffic engineering waypoint, and the RFC defines new SRv6 endpoint behaviors for mobile-specific functions.
tldr.outcome: Mobile networks can use SRv6 to simplify user-plane operations, reduce per-session state, enable flexible traffic engineering and network slicing, and support virtualized functions without protocol overhead.

facts.label: New SRv6 endpoint behaviors
facts.value: 6 defined: End.MAP, End.M.GTP6.D, End.M.GTP6.D.Di, End.M.GTP6.E, End.M.GTP4.E, H.M.GTP4.D, End.Limit

facts.label: Deployment modes
facts.value: Traditional, Enhanced, GTP-U interworking (IPv6 and IPv4)

today: RFC 9433 is an Informational RFC published in July 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It documents the applicability of SRv6 to mobile networks and defines specific endpoint behaviors and deployment modes. Several mobile operators have begun piloting SRv6 in their networks, and the mechanisms are suitable for both greenfield and evolutionary deployments alongside GTP-U.

sections.title: The Mobile User Plane Today
sections.content: Mobile networks provide connectivity to mobile devices by establishing tunnels through a backhaul and core network from the device to an anchor point. The current architecture uses GTP-U (GPRS Tunnelling Protocol User Plane) to tunnel each user session. This approach has drawbacks: it maintains per-session tunneling state, it does not allow operators to optimize the data path end-to-end, and it separates the user plane from the underlying transport. Mobile networks are becoming more challenging to operate due to rising traffic, lower latency requirements, distributed virtualized functions, and a growing number of devices creating scalability issues. Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) offers an alternative. SRv6 is the IPv6 instantiation of Segment Routing, where a source node steers a packet through an ordered list of instructions called segments. Applied to mobile networks, SRv6 enables source routing of mobile user-plane traffic, stateless operation, and integration of transport and service layers, all without protocol overhead.
sections.eli5: Today's phone networks put each call in its own private tunnel and remember a lot of details about each call. SRv6 is like just telling the packet which stops to make, and it goes on the regular network.

sections.title: SRv6 Mobile User Plane Modes
sections.content: RFC 9433 defines multiple deployment modes. Traditional mode is the simplest: it replaces GTP-U with SRv6 while keeping the 3GPP control plane unchanged. A unique SRv6 SID is assigned per PDU Session, replacing each GTP-U tunnel. The N3 (gNB to UPF), N9 (UPF to UPF), and N6 (UPF to data network) interfaces use point-to-point SRv6 paths with no intermediate waypoints. This minimizes changes to the mobile system. Enhanced mode goes further: it allows multiple SIDs in the SID list for traffic engineering, service programming, and device aggregation. Intermediate waypoints can include traffic engineering nodes or VNFs (Virtual Network Functions) transparent to 3GPP. This improves scalability, enables end-to-end network slicing, and provides SLA control. The RFC also describes three interworking modes for legacy gNBs still using GTP-U, allowing gradual migration to SRv6. In all modes, SRv6 operates statelessly: the path is encoded in the packet, and intermediate nodes process it without maintaining session state.
sections.eli5: In the simple version, we replace tunnels with source routing, one path per call. In the fancy version, we can add extra stops for traffic control or services, and handle many calls the same way. Old networks can keep using GTP-U while new networks use SRv6.

sections.title: SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors for Mobility
sections.content: RFC 9433 defines new SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors to support mobile functions. End.MAP is used by intermediate UPFs to map (replace) an arriving SID with the next SID in the list, advancing the packet to the next waypoint. Args.Mob.Session is an argument format embedded in SIDs to carry per-session information (QFI, PDU Session ID, reflective QoS indication) when one SID aggregates multiple sessions. End.M.GTP6.D, End.M.GTP6.D.Di, and End.M.GTP6.E are used in IPv6/GTP-U interworking: they decapsulate GTP-U, push an SRv6 header with a SID list, or encapsulate back to GTP-U. End.M.GTP4.E and H.M.GTP4.D provide similar functions for IPv4/GTP-U interworking, using SID encoding to carry IPv4 addresses and TEIDs. End.Limit enforces rate limiting based on group identifiers and rate values in the SID. These behaviors operate on control plane information and do not require special security consideration beyond the SR domain security model.
sections.eli5: Different routers know different tricks. Some know how to swap one address for another. Some know how to convert between old GTP tunnels and new SRv6. Some know how to slow down traffic. Each trick is a named behavior.

sections.title: How Traffic Flows in SRv6 Mobile
sections.content: In Traditional mode uplink, a device sends a packet to its gateway (gNB). The gNB encapsulates it into IPv6 with a single SID (the anchor UPF) and no Segment Routing Header since there is only one segment. The packet reaches the UPF, which is configured with End.MAP and replaces the destination address with the next UPF's SID, then forwards it. The final UPF performs decapsulation and table lookup, then forwards to the data network. In downlink, traffic arrives at the final UPF destined to the device; the UPF finds the session's SID list and encapsulates it into IPv6 with the SRH pointing to the device. Intermediate UPFs use End.MAP to decrement the hop limit and map to the next SID. In Enhanced mode, multiple services or traffic engineering waypoints are included in the initial SID list, and each node performs its function (service processing or traffic engineering) before forwarding to the next segment. The stateless nature of SRv6 means each node independently processes the packet based on the SID and SRH, requiring no per-session state except at the anchor points.
sections.eli5: Uplink: the phone attaches an address label saying which anchor to go to, and middle routers just change the label to the next stop. Downlink: the anchor attaches the whole path, and each router follows the path to the next stop until it reaches the phone.

sections.title: Flexibility and Network Slicing
sections.content: A key advantage of SRv6 is flexibility in path selection and network slicing. Different PDU sessions can use different SID lists based on SLA requirements, allowing separation of high-priority and best-effort traffic. IGP Flex-Algo (Flexible Algorithm) can be used to compute paths for specific slices, and On-Demand Next Hop (ODN) with Automated Steering can provision slice-specific paths dynamically. SRv6 supports all 3GPP PDU Session Types: IPv4, IPv6, IPv4v6, Ethernet, and Unstructured. Sessions use corresponding SRv6 endpoint behaviors (End.DX4, End.DT4, End.DX6, End.DT6, End.DT46, End.DX2) without per-type tunneling overhead. Session aggregation allows multiple UEs sharing the same SID list if they have identical requirements, reducing the number of SIDs compared to GTP-U's per-session TEID approach. The control plane remains unchanged: SMF (Session Management Function) signals QoS rules and policies as before, and gNB and UPF use local policy to instantiate SRv6 accordingly.
sections.eli5: You can have different paths for different kinds of calls—fast paths for video, normal paths for web, slow paths for background data. One path can carry many calls at once. The control messages stay the same; only how we carry the data changes.
